opening.headline: We cover how to solve the hassle of re-uploading the same file every time you ask a question with projects and knowledge spaces that collect materials and instructions in one place.
body: Post a price list on Monday to ask a question, then open a new chat on Tuesday and post the same price list again. PDFs of company regulations, price lists, and minutes of past meetings are scattered across email, Drive, and messenger, and each team member uploads a different version of the file, giving different answers to the same question.

In this class, we will sequentially look at what a project that bundles chat, knowledge files, and instructions in one place is and how it is structured, how to increase the limit and size of materials that can be uploaded, and how to determine the scope of sharing. Next, we compare the composition of Gemini Notebook, a source-based research tool, and the three products in the same framework, and finally, we decide where to place the price list and company regulations according to the frequency of update.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of knowledge spaces such as projects and notebooks
Uploaded data and real-time connected data can be classified according to update frequency.
Can describe the constraints that context windows and RAGs place on how the model writes data

screens.title: Re-upload the file every time you ask a question
screens.lead: This is a scene where the same file is uploaded to each chat. Read below and think about the hassles and risks.

visual.alt: A scene where the same three PDFs are repeatedly attached to each chat window on different days of the week.

paragraphs: A sales representative posted a price list on AI chat on Monday morning and asked for a quote. The next day I open a new chat and the AI ​​doesn't know the price list I posted yesterday. This is because the model does not remember the content between conversations, the principle of which will be examined in detail in the middle of this lesson. Raise the same price tag again. Including PDFs of company regulations and past meeting minutes, there are days when the same file is uploaded three or four times a day.

Materials are scattered across email, Drive, and Messenger, and each team member uploads a different version. One person posted last month's price list and another person posted this month's price list, so even the same question will have different answers. You can find out which answer is correct by checking the version of the file separately.

The question for this class is this. What is the space for gathering materials and guidance in one place, and how should it be organized? Having that space eliminates repetitive uploads and allows your team to work from the same material.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Although it is convenient to collect data in one place, you must also consider whether the data will be out of date and who can view it.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the problem of repetition, let's think about how you store your data.

screens.title: Remember how you store your data
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever posted the same file repeatedly to multiple chats?
items.answer: Most have at least once. Chats are essentially independent of each conversation, so files are needed again for each conversation. Projects try to eliminate this repetition by placing files outside of the conversation.

items.prompt: After modifying the data, has the AI ever been left with an old version?
items.answer: Since the uploaded file is a copy at that time, it is not automatically copied even if the original is modified. This distinction is one of the keys to this lesson, and whether you keep a copy or link to the original will determine how often the material changes.

items.prompt: When sharing team material, do you ever worry about who can see it?
items.answer: Deciding the scope of sharing is as important as convenience. When you create a project in Team and Enterprise plans, Claude lets you choose whether it's visible to the entire organization or only to those you invite. For details on how to distinguish between public scopes, see the screen dealing with sharing scopes.

screens.outro: Let's first look at the components of the project.

screens.title: Projects: Chat, files, and instructions in one place
screens.lead: You can see a detailed description of each component of the project by selecting the number marker above the picture.

visual.alt: Schematic of a project box containing four compartments: chat, knowledge files, instructions, and saved responses.
labels: Knowledge files (PDF, spreadsheet, document, image, text)
Project guidelines (applies only within this project)

markers.label: What is a project?
markers.title: Workspace to group related tasks
markers.body:
The ChatGPT help explains that ChatGPT keeps all chats, files, and instructions related to your project in one place so they all stay in the same context. You can start on one device, continue on another, and reuse it for recurring tasks like weekly research or content drafts.

In Claude, projects are independent workspaces with their own chat history and knowledge base. Both products are similar in that they unite tasks rather than single conversations.

markers.label: knowledge file
markers.title: Data on which the answer is based
markers.body:
You can upload PDFs, spreadsheets, documents, images, or paste text into your project as reference material. ChatGPT provides a more knowledgeable answer based on the content you posted. Files can be opened, downloaded, or deleted from the project's source list.

If you upload a file with the same name, you will be prompted to choose between 'Upload anyway' and 'Skip'. When uploading multiple files at once, only the conflicting files will be skipped and the rest will continue to upload.

markers.label: Project Guidelines
markers.title: Rules that only apply within this project
markers.body:
You can write down instructions in your project settings. For example, write something like, ‘Act like a marketing mentor, write concisely, use bullet points, and ask questions back.’ ChatGPT help explains that project instructions apply only within that project and take precedence over global Custom instructions.

Therefore, it is safe to place criteria that are specific to specific tasks in project guidelines rather than global guidelines.

markers.label: saved response
markers.title: Returning good results to data
markers.body:
Save one response as a project resource so you can reuse it in the next chat. Once a well-organized summary or table has been created, there is no need to create a new one every time.

However, the saved response is also a copy at that point in time. If the original material has changed, you should check whether the saved responses are out of date.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the components, let's look at ways to increase the limits and scale of the material.

screens.title: Context Window: What the model sees at once
screens.lead: Select the arrows to step through the steps to see what the model actually looks at to answer, what happens when you have more data, and how RAG solves it.

visual.alt: A schematic showing the context window being divided into five sections and the RAG flow in which only relevant pieces from the data storage are entered into the window.
labels: Context window (how much to read at a time)
Outside the window: the model doesn't see it
Retrieve only fragments relevant to your question (RAG)
The file uploaded yesterday will not be visible unless it is included in this request.

steps.title: The model only sees the text of this request
steps.body:
Each time a language model receives a request, it reads the text contained in the request and creates an answer. The model itself has no memory of storing past conversations. This is why the price list posted yesterday is not known today.

In order for the old data to be used in the new chat, the product must include it again in this request and hand it to the model. All the model sees is the text it receives, and any content it doesn't receive is as if it doesn't exist.

steps.title: The context window is the amount read at a time.
steps.body:
The maximum amount of text a model can read at one time is called the context window. Instructions, uploaded materials, conversations so far, new questions, and even the answers the model will write are all shared in this one window.

So, as the data grows, there is less room for conversation and answers. Window size varies by model. Instead of memorizing numbers, this class focuses on how the principle of a limited window limits data organization.

steps.title: When it gets longer, it gets pushed out or the middle becomes weak.
steps.body:
If the volume exceeds the window, older frontiers may be cut out or abridged to reduce the volume. Even if everything goes inside the window, you can't feel safe.

A study by Liu et al. reported that in long inputs, the model tended to use information at the beginning and the end more, and less so at the information in the middle. The degree varies from model to model, but this means that even if a lot of data is included, not all content is reflected with the same weight. It is better to exclude unnecessary data and keep important rules concise.

steps.title: RAG: Retrieve only relevant fragments and place them in the window
steps.body:
When there is too much data to fit in the window, the data is divided into small pieces and stored, and when a question comes in, only the pieces that seem relevant are found and placed in the window. This method is called Search Augmentation Generation, or RAG for short.

The study proposed by Lewis et al. under this name in 2020 consisted of using searches from external document collections in addition to the knowledge stored within the model. The RAG discussed in this class has the same principle. Instead of reading the whole thing, you pick out the parts you need and read them.

steps.title: So the answer can only be based on part
steps.body:
In RAG, all the model sees are the pieces picked by the search. If the search misses a needed piece, it will not be reflected in the answer, even if the material contains the answer. Also, questions that require the entire data, such as 'Compare and summarize the entire data,' may be answered by only looking at part of it.

Therefore, be specific in your question about which document you are looking at and compare important figures with the original text. If the data is within the limit, it is more reliable to read it in its entirety without relying on search.

screens.outro: Now that we know how creatives work, let's look at limits and scaling.

ext.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (Lewis et al.)
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (Liu et al.)

screens.title: Knowledge files, file limits, and scaling
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how the model writes data changes when the amount of knowledge is low, near the context limit, and when it crosses the limit and switches to a search mode.

visual.alt: A bar diagram showing the transition from the whole input method to the RAG method of retrieving only the necessary parts depending on the amount of knowledge.
labels: Search and insert only the necessary parts (RAG)

data.controlLabel: Amount of knowledge contributed to the project

stops.body:
If the uploaded data falls far short of the context limit, the model can view and respond to all data at once. In this state, whatever is in the data is sent to the model along with the question.

Limits vary by product and plan. For the ChatGPT project, the number of files that can be uploaded varies depending on the plan, and Gemini Notebook advises that each source can upload up to 500,000 words or 200MB of uploaded files, and free users can upload up to 50 sources. The basic rule is to only use documents for which you have the rights.

As data accumulates and you approach the context limit, you have less time to answer because the data and conversation share the same window. As the question becomes longer or the conversation continues, the first part may get pushed aside.

What is needed at this time is to select only the parts relevant to the question instead of including all the data. You can also organize files to remove unnecessary material or divide a project into work units.

Claude project documentation explains that on paid plans, when project knowledge approaches context limits, it automatically switches to RAG mode, expanding capacity by up to 10x. RAG is a method that searches only parts related to the question and puts them into context.

This method allows you to use a lot of material that cannot be contained in its entirety. Instead, keep in mind that the model does not read the entire data each time, but only looks at the part of the data it retrieves, so the answer may be based on only part of the data.

screens.outro: Now that you have your limits, let's look at sharing and visibility.

screens.title: Sharing and Visibility: Public and Private
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare the range of people who can access your project when you make it public and when you make it private.

visual.alt: On the organization chart, an illustration of two states with different access ranges for public and private projects.

states.label: Public (organization-wide)
states.body:
In Claude's Team and Enterprise plans, you first choose a privacy when you create a project. If you select Public, all members of the organization can view and write about the project. Members can start a new chat by finding it in the Organization tab of their project list.

However, even if a project is public, individual chats within the project remain private. What the entire organization sees is the project space - knowledge and guidance, not each individual's conversations.

Public is suitable for spaces where all employees must ask questions based on the same data, such as company regulations. Even after creation, you can change it to Private by pressing the Share button next to the project name.

states.label: Private (invited only)
states.body:
If you select Private, only the person who created it will initially have access. A project's chat, knowledge, and artifacts are not open to members who have not been explicitly invited.

You can invite members and give them view or edit permission using the Share button. You can change Private to Public at any time in the same way. Administrators can also turn off public projects or the project sharing feature itself at the organization level.

Private is suitable for materials that only the responsible team should see, such as the sales team's price list. In ChatGPT, the chats, files, and instructions in a shared project all become a shared context for the team to continue working on. When you delete a file from a shared project, it is deleted for everyone. When sharing, you should also check who can delete what.

data.notes: Gemini Notebook is a research tool that posts sources and answers with inline citations based solely on those sources. It is in the same family as the previous renamed tool, and manages data on a notebook basis within the app. The key to reading the table is the update method row. Even if the same word 'Google Drive connection' is used, depending on the product, it may be a source that is automatically synchronized, or it may be an app that can only be searched and accessed. Therefore, when connecting data, first check whether the connection method is synchronization or copy. If you also look at the limit row, you can estimate in advance whether the size and number of materials to be uploaded falls within the product's limits.

screens.outro: Now that we have compared the composition, we move on to the case of dividing the data by update frequency.

screens.title: Case explanation 1: Distinguish between uploaded data and linked data by update frequency
screens.lead: Establish criteria for the instructor to determine whether material should be copied or linked to the original. Select the arrows and follow them step by step.

steps.title: The uploaded file is a copy of the point in time
steps.body: When you upload a file to a project, you have a copy of it at that moment. Basically, even if you modify the original later, the copy in the project does not automatically follow suit. So after fixing it, a person has to replace it with a new file.

steps.title: Linked data is updated when the original changes.
steps.body: Linked materials are updated according to the original. Sources imported from Gemini Notebook to Google Drive automatically sync every few minutes, or you can open the source to sync directly. If you edit the original document, the changes will be reflected when you open the notebook.

steps.title: The meaning of connection is different for each product.
steps.body: The Google Drive app added to a ChatGPT project does not support pre-sync, the help notes. So, it can be searched and accessed, but it is not the same as automatic synchronization of Notebook. You should not judge that it is the same operation just by looking at the word ‘connection’.

steps.title: Judgment axis: update frequency
steps.body: The method is determined by how often the data changes. For data that changes frequently, it is appropriate to link it to the original and update it automatically. It is simple and stable to upload data that rarely changes, make a copy of it, and replace it only when it changes.

steps.title: Check before using a connection method
steps.body: No matter which connection method you choose, you should first check which product actually syncs. If the product is not synchronized, the latest status cannot be guaranteed even if connected, so it is safe to establish a replacement procedure.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the principles, let's put the two materials into practice.

screens.title: Case Commentary 2: Where to put the price list and company regulations
screens.lead: When you select a material card, the location, reason, and sharing scope determined by the instructor are revealed. Please judge for yourself first and then press it.

items.prompt: Pricing list: Sales team materials that change several times a month
items.answer: Since it changes frequently, a space that is synchronized by connecting to the Drive source is appropriate. An example would be something like Gemini Notebook where Drive sources are updated every few minutes. If you keep it on a product that is not synchronized, you must establish a procedure for replacing it with the latest version. The scope of sharing is Private, limited to sales team members.

items.prompt: Company regulations: Data for all employees revised approximately once a year
items.answer: It rarely changes, so you can just place it in your project knowledge file and replace it only when it's revised. Simple and low management burden. Since all employees must ask questions based on the same regulations, the appropriate scope of sharing is Public, which is open to the entire organization.

items.prompt: Common Guidelines: Where should I set my tone and response standards?
items.answer: Leave it to the project guidelines. If you write down criteria such as 'Answer by quoting the provisions of the regulations, and say there is nothing if it is not in the regulations' in the project guidelines, they will apply to all chats in that project. Guidelines are effective only within the project and do not affect other work.

items.prompt: What if you summarize the order of location in one line?
items.answer: The order is to look at the nature of the data, consider the frequency of update, and determine the scope of sharing. The nature determines whether it is evidence or a rule, the update frequency determines whether connection or upload is appropriate, and the sharing scope determines who should be able to view it.

screens.outro: Now that we've explained the layout, let's summarize the main points of this class.

screens.title: Determine location based on the nature of the material
screens.lead: Let's summarize the content covered in this class by connecting it to the first question.

paragraphs: The first question was what would be a space to gather materials and guidance in one place and how would it be organized? The answer is projects. Projects bundle related chats, knowledge files, and instructions, eliminating repetitive uploads and keeping teams working in the same vein. Because guidelines only apply within that project, you can safely set task-specific standards.

There are three things to consider when organizing a space. The nature of the material, how frequently it is updated, and the extent to which it is shared. Materials that change frequently are linked and synchronized with the original, and materials that rarely change are uploaded and kept as copies. However, the meaning of connection varies from product to product, so make sure it is actually synchronized.

Sharing is managed by public, private, and permission levels. Even in public projects, individual chats remain private, and private projects can only be viewed by invitees. Don't forget the basics of uploading only documents with rights.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: Before uploading material, decide how often this material will change and who should be able to see it.

checks.q: There is a lot of data in the project, so we are searching and using the RAG method. Which of the following is the best understanding?
options: The model reads the entire material from beginning to end for each question.
Since you only look at and answer fragments retrieved that are relevant to the question, your answer may be based on only part of the data.
The model remembers the data so there is no need to search in new chats.
Because it is a search method, all content in the data is always reflected in the answer.
checks.explain: RAG works by putting only the fragments relevant to the question into the window. Anything your search misses may not be reflected in your answer, so you should check important figures against the original text.

wrong.0: Reading the whole thing is the way it is when the material is at a scale that fits into a window.
wrong.2: The model does not remember content between conversations, and the product must hand over the material with each request.
wrong.3: Pieces that are missing from the search cannot always be reflected because the model does not see them.

wrong.0: Knowledge in public projects is open to organization members.
wrong.1: Instructions are also shared as part of the project space.
wrong.2: Name and privacy are the basic information for sharing.

wrong.0: The synchronization method is suitable for materials such as price lists that change frequently.

glossary.def: A workspace that brings together related chats, files, and instructions in one place.
These guidelines apply only within the project. In ChatGPT, they take precedence over global Custom instructions.
This is material that can be uploaded to a project or notebook and used as the basis for an answer.
This method searches only parts related to the question and puts them into context. It is used to increase capacity when knowledge approaches its limit.
This is Google's research tool that provides answers with citations based on posted sources.
The maximum amount of text the model can read at one time. Instructions, materials, conversations, and answers all share this one window.

misconceptions.myth: Files uploaded to the project are automatically reflected when the original is modified.
misconceptions.fact: Uploaded files are copies of the files at the time they were uploaded. The method of automatically renewing connections varies from product to product, so you'll need to check whether they are synchronized or not.

misconceptions.myth: If you make the project public, all chats within it will be visible.
misconceptions.fact: Even if it is public, individual chats within a project remain private. What the entire organization sees is the project space.

misconceptions.myth: Project guidelines apply to all my conversations.
misconceptions.fact: Project guidelines apply only to conversations within that project. You will need to write global or account-wide guidelines to apply them to all conversations.

misconceptions.myth: AI remembers files and conversations uploaded yesterday.
misconceptions.fact: The model itself does not remember anything between conversations. The reason that previous data is used is because the product returns that data in this request.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Projects bundle chat, knowledge files, and instructions to eliminate repetitive uploads.
Project guidelines apply only within that project.
Sharing is managed by public, private, and permission levels, and individual chats remain private even in public projects.
Determine the location of uploaded and linked materials based on the frequency of updates.

closing.reflection: What files do I repeatedly upload to AI in my work, and how often do they change?
